title: A Magnon-photon interface based on Van der Waals Magnetic semiconductor

paper_content.abstract: Coherent control of light with electron spins represents a fundamental goal across multiple research fields, such as opto-spintronics, chiroptics, quantum information. In a magnetic-ordered material, coherent magnon gives rise to temporally and spatially modulated spin structure that may stimulate intriguing spin-photon interactions as well as opto-spintronic applications. However, the development of such magnon-photon interface is hampered due to the lack of magnetic photonic structure that embraces strong light-matter interaction. Here, we present such magnon-photon interface in a CrSBr metasurface by showing the formation of a magnetic exciton polariton bound states in the continuum, whose energy and the radiative properties can be tuned with an external magnetic field. We further show that the exciton polaritons are modulated by the coherent magnon excitation, exhibiting a nontrivial magnon mode- and k-dependent behavior which suggests the formation of hybrid magnon-exciton polariton states. Our results shed light on the interplay of spin, magnon and photon in the magnetic metasurface and provide a new platform for exploring spin functional photonic and quantum devices.
paper_content.introduction:
The electron spin carries non-volatile quantum information, which has been widely explored for information storage and processing1–5. Interfacing the spin states with photons allows communication and detection of spin quantum information over long distance6–9. Such spin-photon interface is therefore critical to connecting spatially separated quantum nodes and has been recognized as a vital part of the vision for scalable spin quantum information.

Significant progress has been made for non-magnetic spin-photon interface. This includes development of high-fidelity spin-photon entangled states, photons switches, routers and efficient chiral emitters controlled by electron spin in III-V semiconductor quantum dots7,9,10, transition metal dichalcogenide11–13 as well as scalable on-chip integration of optically active defect spins in diamond and SiC8,14,15. The non-magnetic semiconductor nanostructures and color centers are benefited from the optically active materials and long spin coherence time16,17. Whereas, magnetic materials, although being the backbone of contemporary spintronic research and memory industry, are less explored due to optically inactive band-edge transitions18,19, degraded optical properties20,21, as well as limited spin relaxation and coherence time22,23.

Recently, the discovery of magnetic semiconductors, e.g., CrSBr, with strong light-matter interaction and intriguing magneto-electronic coupling effect has revived the hope for developing a spin-photon interface that allows harvesting the versatility of spin manipulation and magnetic phase engineering in a magnetic material24–30. Additionally, magnon arises as a unique wave-like spin excitation in magnetically ordered materials31. In CrSBr, magnon is found strongly coupled to the excitonic states, reshaping its optical properties in the ultrafast timescale32,33. Despite the development, two major obstacles persist. First of all, studies of magnon-exciton interactions in 2D magnetic semiconductors have only been conducted in structureless samples which mostly involving interaction with free-space photons. Carefully designed photonic structures, e.g., photonic cavity or metasurfaces with high quality factor or strong magneto-optical response, will likely not only enhance the spin-photon interaction but also provide extra tunability34–36. In particular, photonic structures hosting bound states in the continuum (BICs) have attracted great attention due to their potential to achieve infinite-high cavity Q factors and sensitive to external perturbations, giving rise to intriguing light-matter interaction that facilitate the low threshold lasing, ultrafast optical switches, etc37–39. Coupling of the non-local BICs mode with the local excitation in the magnetic materials, e.g., excitons, may also give access to significant tunability through interplay of the local and non-local transition of the system40,41. Secondly, the fundamental physics underlying the coupling between collective spin waves and photons is not well understood. Although the propagation of magnons in CrSBr has been confirmed42,43, its interaction with the excitonic states is probed in a momentum-integrated manner. A momentum-resolved perspectives are therefore highly appreciated to shed light on the exotic nature of the magnon-photon coupling.

In this work, we demonstrate a magnon-photon interface based on a 1D metasurface of the magnetic semiconductor CrSBr. The CrSBr metasurface hosts BICs that are strongly coupled with excitons forming exciton polaritons (EPs). Owing to the magneto-electronic coupling effect of CrSBr and photonic singularity of the BICs mode, both the energy and the reflectivity of the half-light, half-matter state can be efficiently tuned with an external magnetic field. Furthermore, by performing the transient angle-resolved reflectance spectroscopy on the CrSBr metasurface, we find that the coherent magnon introduces a non-trivial k-dependent oscillation of EP energies that behaves differently for acoustic and optical magnons. These results highlight the wave nature of the magnon-photon coupling in the CrSBr metasurface, which establishes an innovative approach for controlling the photonic or polaritonic devices with electron spins.
paper_content.results:
Magnon-photon interface combining magneto-optical effect and photonic BICs

Figure 1a illustrates the proposed magnon-photon interface made from a CrSBr grating, in which the reflected light of frequency ωph and momentum k is coupled to the transverse electric (TE) mode of the grating and is modulated by a launched coherent magnon. The bulk CrSBr is an A-type antiferromagnetic semiconductor with Néel temperature TN = 132 K. The orientation of the antiferromagnetically coupled macrospins S1 and S2 in the adjacent layers has strong impact on the excitonic structure as well as optical response of the material. By applying an external magnetic field of B = 3 T along the c-axis, S1 and S2 switch from anti-parallel (AP) to parallel (P) spin configuration as shown in Fig. 1b. As a result, the b-axis dielectric function εb = ε1 + iε2 of CrSBr is modified drastically as shown in Fig. 1c, d. Here, εb is extracted from the reflectance spectra with details given in Supplementary Note 1 and Fig. S1. The multi-resonance reflectance features in Fig. S1 is due to the multi-order Fabry-Perot resonances arise from the planar cavity formed between the top and bottom surface of the CrSBr flake and is therefore not reflected by the fitted εb in Fig. 1c, d. The giant magneto-optical response is caused by spin mediated interlayer coupling, leading to a prominent redshift of the 1s exciton state from X(0) = 1.3643 eV to X(B) = 1.3485 eV as marked in Fig. 1d. Such magneto-electronic effect stems from the exchange interaction and is expected to have a stronger impact than typical magneto-optical effects, e.g., Faraday, Kerr rotation, etc., which are received from the spin orbital interaction44. In Fig. 1e, we show the calculated TE mode dispersion of the proposed CrSBr grating. Owing to the strong light-matter interaction, the shown eigenmodes are essentially EPs hybridized between the 1s exciton and guided resonances (GRs). The Γ point of the TE1 mode as marked in Fig. 1e is a BICs with topological charge C = +1, evidenced by divergent Q factor and the far-field polarization map as shown in Fig. 1f. The corresponding mode distribution can be found in Supplementary Fig. S2. The BICs mode is often considered as photonic singularity which is inherited with strong tunability. However, to our knowledge, its role in a magnetic metasurface as the one shown here has not yet been explored.

Strong coupling of exciton and BICs mode in a CrSBr 1D grating

The optical and atomic force microscopy (AFM) image of the exfoliated CrSBr flake is shown in Fig. 2a, b. The polarization-resolved photoluminescence (PL) spectra in Fig. 2c reveal emissions from a series of self-hybridized EPs that are linearly polarized along the b-axis. The coupling strength is estimated to be ~ 167 meV by fitting the emission peak position with a coupled oscillator model (COM) as shown in Fig. 2d (see Supplementary Note 2 and Fig. S3).

Next, the CrSBr metasurface is fabricated by patterning the CrSBr flakes with e-beam lithography followed by dry etching. The grating grooves are aligned along the b-axis of the crystal to maximize the coupling strength. In Fig. 2e, the scanning electron microscope (SEM) image shows that the bottom part of the CrSBr flake is still connected, allowing the continuous propagation of spin wave throughout the whole structure. Figure 2f shows the angle-resolved reflectance (ARR) spectrum taken from the CrSBr metasurface at 10 K, which is nicely matched to the simulated ARR spectrum in Fig. 2g. In Supplementary Fig. S4, we show the ARR spectrum from a CrSBr metasurface with the same structure parameters while the grating grooves are along a-axis. In this case, the photonic modes are decoupled from the exciton, giving rise to markedly different dispersion as in Fig. S4. Furthermore, we have carried out analysis based on COM and the simulation results are shown in Fig. S5. The COM suggests that a coupling strength of ~ 186 meV is needed to reproduce the observed polariton dispersion and the strong coupling is also reached in the CrSBr grating sample. We note that the slightly increase of the fitting values for the coupling strength as well as exciton oscillator strength (see table S1) for the CrSBr grating as compared to the bulk sample is likely artificially caused by the Lorentzian dielectric model25,26 which neglects the energy dependence of the background dielectric constant εb0. A more accurate determination of the coupling strength requires a more realistic modeling of the dielectric function over large spectral range. Nevertheless, the obtained comparable exciton oscillator strength for the etched and unetched sample suggest that the optical quality of the CrSBr grating is not compromised by etching. The EPs at around 1.27 eV in Fig. 2f features a bright and dark state (BS and DS) at Γ point (θ = 0) separated by a gap of ~ 8 meV. The same spectral feature is observed in the angle-resolved PL (ARPL) spectrum in Fig. 3a. The EPs emission intensity diminishes at the vicinity of the DS, accompanied by the increase of the Q factor as shown in Fig. 3b. The DS and BS are identified as the TE1 and TE2 EP. The two modes are slightly redshifted compared from the eigenmode calculation in Fig. 1e due to the presence of the SiO/Si substrate. The absence of the PL and reflectance contrast of the DS is due to the symmetry-forbidden emission of the BICs at θ = 0°. In the following content, we will refer to the exciton polariton formed by the strong coupling between the BICs mode and CrSBr excitons as EP BICs for short.

Tuning the exciton polariton BICs with magnetic field

The formation of EP BICs facilitates the control of its optical response by manipulating the spin configuration. Applying an out-of-plane magnetic field tilts the macrospins S1 and S2 as illustrated in Fig. 3c. The change of spin configuration modulates the energy of the EPs. As shown in Fig. 3d, the BS redshifts with magnetic field and reaches saturation at B = 2.1 T. The total energy change of the BS ΔEBS = 13.1 meV is huge considering the field induced total energy shift of 1s exciton is about 4Eex = 15.8 meV. The large energy shift is consistent with the substantial exciton fraction of the EP which is estimated |X|2 = (|X|2 + |C|2) = 0.39 using the coupled oscillator model. Here, X and C are the exciton and photon part of the Hopfield coefficients for the lower polariton branch45.

Interestingly, The EP BICs which is completely dark in the ARR measurement in the absence of magnetic field, start to red shifts and develops a reflectance feature with applying magnetic field. The brightening of EP BICs is further illustrated in Fig. 3e, where two resonant features are identified at B = 3 T and fitted with Fano lineshape. The dashed and solid arrows mark the fitted resonant energies of the bright and dark state. Table S2 in the supplementary information summarizes the fitting parameters for the two resonances. As guided by the fitting curves, the dark state locates at about 8 meV above the bright state and exhibits a highly asymmetric lineshape. As a comparison, only the resonant feature of the BS is observed and fitted for spectrum measured at B = 0 T in Fig. 3e.

An out-of-plane magnetic field contributes to a sizable off-diagonal dielectric tensor element εab = ε0ab + iε0ab (see Supplementary Note 3 and Fig. S6)46. εab introduces coupling between GRs and broad FP resonances, that can potentially affects the reflectance spectrum in field. Ideally the Γ-point BICs is strictly radiatively forbidden. The robustness of the BICs is protected by the C2 symmetry which holds even in the presence of magnetic field. This is shown with simulated reflectance spectrum in Fig. 3f in which the reflectance features of BICs is absent at different ε0ab for a perfect grating with infinite periods. However, the translation symmetry is broken due to limited sample size or white light spot size. As a result, the reflectance at θ = 0° mixes in the contributions from near-Γ quasi-BICs at finite k. Considering system dimension of ~ 20 μm limited by beam size, it leads to a k-space blurriness of Δθ ~ 1.4° as estimated with the uncertainty relation Δk · Δx ≥ 1/2. Such near-Γ contribution is simulated in Fig. 3g, h for θ = 0.3° and 0.6°. It is evident that the reflectance features of the quasi-BICs state (DS) gradually build up with the increase of ε0ab within the uncertainty limit of Δθ, which is consistent with the experimental observation of the brightened BICs in Fig. 3d and e. In Fig. S7, we further show from simulation that the field-induced reflectance features from the quasi-BICs depends on both real and imaginary part of εab and generally leads to asymmetric Fano lineshape as observed in the experiment. The observed intriguing magneto-optical effect emerges exclusively at the magnetic EP-BICs, which is due to the combined effect of the magnetic field induced εab and the fact that the quasi-BICs is sensitive to such external perturbation. In Supplementary Fig. S8, as a comparison, we show that the reflectance amplitude is barely changed for other EPs that are far apart from the BICs point.

k-dependent magnon-exciton polariton interaction

Next, we turn to the EPs that are closer to the exciton resonance which maximize the magnon-photon interaction. A transient ARR (tr-ARR) spectroscopy is employed to study the interaction between the EPs and coherent magnons in the CrSBr metasurface. The tr-ARR monitors the time evolution of the pump induced ARR change ΔR/R(θ, Eprobe) which are function of both the probe light energy Eprobe and θ. Our measurement configuration is shown in Fig. 4a. A constant magnetic field of 0.48 T is applied to cant the interlayer spins which facilitate exciton-magnon coupling25. Figure 4b shows a typical tr-ARR spectrum measured at 14 K and t = 47 ps. Here, the ΔR/R is mainly caused by pump induced redshift of the EPs, which is opposite to the typical blueshift observed for EPs nonlinearity in non-magnetic materials47,48. The effect is pronounced for EPs derived from the FP mode at around 1.35 eV and multiple GRs in between 1.3-1.34 eV. We attribute the ΔR/R signal to the excitation of incoherent magnon, which contributes to the decreases of EP energies and decays slowly with time as shown in Supplementary Fig. S9. Apart from the incoherent component, the coherent magnon excitation is also observed as the temporal oscillation of the ΔR/R. In the upper panel of Fig. 4c, the coherent oscillation of the tr-ARR (CoTR) is made pronounced by taking the time derivative of ΔR/R and is plotted as function of Eprobe and t for θ = 0°. The oscillations take opposite phase for Eprobe above and below the EP resonances. It suggests that the EP energies are periodically modulated through interaction with coherent magnon, which is consistent with previous report in pristine CrSBr flakes32. In the lower panel of Fig. 4c, CoTR at probe energy (Eprobe = 1.3536 eV) slightly above the 1.35-eV EP is plotted against time, exhibiting clear oscillations with a beating amplitude.

To gain in-depth understanding of the coherent magnon-EP dynamics, we performed fast Fourier transformation (FFT) of the CoTR signal for each Eprobe and the results for different θ are shown in Fig. 4e. In the FFT spectra, two dominant oscillation frequencies at 30 GHz and 22 GHz are identified and attributed to the acoustic and optical magnon modes (marked as Ac. and Op.). The corresponding mode character featured by the in-phase and out-of-phase precession of the macrospin S1 and S2 of the neighboring antiferromagnetically coupled layers is illustrated in Fig. 4d. In Fig. 4f, the FFT magnitude at the two magnon mode frequencies is plotted against θ. The FFT magnitude at the frequency of optical magnon decreases at higher |θ|, whereas the acoustic magnon contribution remains at a comparable level for all θ in our measurements. The k-dependent coupling between EP and optical magnon modes cannot be otherwise explained by any k-space dependence of the EP, which is shown to be similar for both magnon modes. It has been suggested that the transient strain field generated by the pump light plays important roles for launching magnon in CrSBr and the k-space distribution of the coherent magnon should be limited by the Fourier transformation of the real-space transient strain field42. In our measurement, the pump laser was defocused to a large laser spot size of ~ 10 μm. It therefore generates a broad real-space heat/strain profile. The dashed line in Fig. 4f estimate the contribution of heat/strain by showing the Fourier transformation of the real-space laser spot profile, which is too narrow to account for the observation of the broad k-space profile for the optical magnon. It suggests that the EP oscillations ΔE(t) ∝ Δm(t) ∝ Δm(t) where ΔE(t) is the relative angle between S1(t) and S2(t) for the exciton energy difference between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phase. The magnon-photon interactions observed here are beyond the conventional heat/strain-mediated mechanism which is often responsible for magnon-photon interaction in magnetic materials or devices. Furthermore, the optical magnon has a similar profile as the angular distribution of the pump density (Fig. 4f). It is worth to know that such angular distribution of the pump density deviates from the Fourier transformed real-space profile of the pump beam due to the defocused pump laser beam setting. This is a strong indication for a k-conserved coupling between EP and the optical magnons such that the momentum is transferred to the magnon mode upon optical excitation. However, such momentum conservation law does not hold for acoustic magnons. We note that the similar k-conserved behavior of the optical magnon is also observed for measurement in pristine CrSBr as shown in Fig. 4g, h. However, a noteworthy difference in the unpatterned CrSBr is that the acoustic mode is absent in the FFT spectra at all angles.

To shed light on the different k-space behavior of the optical and acoustic magnons, we solved the Landau-Lifshitz equation describing the time evolution of sublattice magnetization mi=1,2(t) of bulk CrSBr as illustrated in Fig. 5a,

dmi(t)/dt = -γμ0 mi(t) × Hi,eff (1)

Here, γ and μ0 are gyromagnetic ratio and vacuum permeability. Hi,eff is the effective magnetic field of mi=1,2(t) and includes contributions from Zeeman interaction, interlayer exchange coupling and the magnetic anisotropy (detailed derivation is given in Supplementary Note 4). Assuming the reported interaction parameters, Fig. 5b shows the calculated mode frequencies for acoustic and optical magnons as function of the c-axis magnetic field32. It is established that the modulation of the CrSBr exciton and exciton polariton energies ΔE is proportional to the time-varying angle between S1(t) and S2(t). Figure 5c, d calculate the temporal modulation of ΔE at zero and finite magnetic field assuming either acoustic or optical magnon is excited. At Hext = 0, neither acoustic nor optical magnon is coupled to the exciton or EPs, as evidenced by the absence of ΔE at the magnon frequency ω in Fig. 5c. However, weak higher order frequency component at 2ω is identified for both magnons. A finite magnetic field, e.g., μ0Hext = 0.48 T, initiates the coupling between the exciton and the optical mode as shown by the emerging oscillation of ΔE at ω in Fig. 5d. Whereas, the acoustic mode remains decoupled at frequency ω. Such distinct selection rules for acoustic and optical magnons in bulk CrSBr nicely explain the absence of the acoustic magnon in the FFT spectra for the unetched CrSBr sample (Fig. 4g, h). The observation of disallowed acoustic magnon in the FFT spectra for CrSBr grating (Fig. 4e, f) then must arise from the etched edges and sidewalls which have low symmetry. At such localized site, the acoustic magnon-exciton polariton interaction therefore does not conserve k and naturally leads to an insensitive dependence on angle. On the other hand, the selection-rules-allowed optical mode requires match of momentum owing to the preserved translation symmetry and therefore leads to an angle-sensitive behavior for both the pristine CrSBr flake and the CrSBr grating. The mode- and k-dependent magnon-EP interaction may indicate the formation of strongly coupled EP-magnon hybrid such that a k-selected excitation of the EPs directly leads to the k-dependent pumping of the coherent magnons which in turn modulates the EPs energies. Such mechanism is therefore sensitive to the character of the magnons in the way that favors the direct optical magnon-EP coupling through the induced angle change between adjacent interlayer macrospins.

We note that controlling light with electron spins has strong implications in spin quantum information and spintronics, which is generally difficult for conventional meta-surfaces or polaritonic devices based on non-magnetic materials. Towards such goal, we have demonstrated both static and ultrafast control of exciton polariton with electron spin or collective modes of spins in a magnetic photonic structure of CrSBr, by harnessing the synergistic interplay between strong light-matter interactions and magneto-electronic effects. Furthermore, the observation of 2D magnon mode- and k-dependent EP interaction provides a compelling evidence of direct momentum transfer from pump photons to the optical magnons, suggesting the formation of strongly coupled magnon-EP hybrid state. These findings provide valuable information for the spin- and magnon-photon interactions in the 2D limit and open a new gateway for exploring spin functional photonic and quantum devices with 2D magnetic semiconductors.
paper_content.methods:
Fabrication of CrSBr metasurface
The commercially available CrSBr crystal (from Nanjing MKNANO) was mechanically exfoliated onto a silicon substrate with a 300-nm oxide layer in the glove box, and the thickness was determined using AFM. Electron beam lithography and ICP-RIE were used to partially etch CrSBr, forming a one-dimensional grating. The etched area of the CrSBr flake is 30 μm × 30 μm. The grating structural parameters and roughness of the measured grating sample is characterized by SEM and AFM in Fig. S10.

Angle-resolved reflectance and PL spectroscopy
The optical measurements are conducted with samples loaded into a low-vibration closed-cycle cryostat. For the PL measurement, a 532-nm continue-wave laser was used for excitation. A halogen lamp was used for the reflectance measurement. The PL emission and the reflected light were collected with a long-working-distance objective lens with a numerical aperture of 0.42. The angle-resolved reflectance/PL spectroscopy consists of reflectance/PL spectra for different incidence angle θ, which are performed by projecting the back focal plane of the objective lens to a spectrometer (FHR640) equipped with a Si charge coupled device (CCD) camera.

Transient angle-resolved reflectance spectroscopy
The tr-ARR measurements are performed with a home-built set-up, which is schematically shown in supplementary Fig. S11. A 1-kHz 800-nm pulsed laser is used as pump light. The pulse width is about 150 fs. The probe light is the white light generated by pumping a sapphire plate with the fs laser. The delay time t between the pump light and the white probe light is precisely controlled to yield the time evolution of ΔR/R. The pump energy density is kept low at 5.1 pJ/μm2 to avoid compromising the coherence of the exciton-magnon coupling due to high carrier/exciton density. The pump light intensity is modulated at the frequency of 20 Hz and the k-space image of the pump induced reflectance change is dispersed and recorded with an EMCCD camera (from Raptor Photonics) that is synchronized to the modulation speed. The pump and probe light spot size is about 10 μm.

Numerical simulations
The finite element method (FEM) is employed to simulate the eigenvalues and reflectance spectra of CrSBr photonic structures using a commercially available software (COMSOL Multiphysics). Periodic boundary conditions are applied in the x- and y-directions, while perfectly matched layers (PMLs) are implemented in the z-direction to minimize reflections. The optical anisotropy of the material is modeled using a dielectric tensor,

ε = [εa 0 0; 0 εb 0; 0 0 εc]

where εa = 12, εc = 3.7. To simulate the eigen-energy of polariton bands, the εb is approximated with the Lorentzian mode:

εb(ω) = εb0 + f/(ω2 - iωΓ - E2X/ℏ2) + f*/(ω2 - iωΓ* - E2X*/ℏ2)

with εb0 = 11.1. The contribution of exciton resonance is taken into account with following parameters, EX = 1.364 eV, EX* = 1.379 eV, ℏΓ = 0.7 meV, ℏΓ* = 7.5 meV, ℏf = 1.304 eV, ℏf* = 0.707 eV. The wave equation,

∇ × (∇ × E(ω)) = k20ε(ω)E(ω)

is then solved numerically by matching the frequency of the eigen mode E(ω) with the dielectric function dispersion ε(ω).

To simulate the magneto-optical effect, an off-diagonal gyromagnetic term is introduced into the dielectric tensor as46,

ε = [εa εab 0; -εab εb 0; 0 0 εc]

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript presents an intriguing and mostly experimental study on magnetic exciton-polaritons in a CrSBr
metasurface. Unlike prior works where CrSBr serves solely as a source of magnetic excitons coupled to external photonic
structures or Fabry-Pérot modes in bulk, this work employs CrSBr itself as both the excitonic medium and the photonic
lattice. This dual role enables in-situ engineering of the photonic modes and offers a compelling route for tunable exciton-
polariton properties via external magnetic fields and photonic lattice design. The authors demonstrate tunable reflectance
around the BIC and observe exciton-polariton modulation by magnons using transient angle-resolved reflectance
spectroscopy. These results are likely to attract broad interest and make meaningful contributions to the study of hybrid
magnon-polariton systems in magnetic semiconductors.
However, several points require clarification or further support before the manuscript can be considered for publication:
1. Figure 3e shows the experimental results of reflectance at θ=0 to illustrate the brightening of dark BIC mode with applied
magnetic field. This observation appears inconsistent with the statement that "the robustness of the BIC is protected by the
C₂ symmetry, which holds even in the presence of magnetic field." This inconsistency should be addressed more clearly.
Moreover, although the role of the off-diagonal dielectric tensor element εab is invoked to explain the effect, simulations are
only shown at a finite angle (θ=2.3). What is the predicted effect of εab at Γ (θ = 0°)? Does it agree with the experimental data
shown in Fig. 3e?
2. In Fig. 4f, the authors present two very different k-space distributions for the pump: one as the "Fourier transform of the
real-space pump pulse" and another as the "measured normalized k-space distribution of the pump light." The notable
discrepancy between these two curves is confusing and should be clearly explained. Additionally, the authors should clarify
how this relates to their argument on the impact of heat/strain and direct momentum transfer mechanisms.
3. The FFT amplitude of the optical and acoustic magnon modes shows different dependence on momentum. Could the
authors provide a more detailed physical explanation of why the optical magnon exhibits stronger k-dependence and why
acoustic magnon does not?
Minor Comments and Suggestions
1. The text description of Fig. 3e seems to refer to Fig. 3f. Please check and revise accordingly.
2. The color bar scale in Fig. 3f uses only "max" and "min" labels. Providing numerical values would better illustrate the
absolute reflectance change attributed to εab.
3. Consider plotting optical and acoustic magnon magnitudes separately in Supplementary Material to more clearly reveal
their different k-dependences.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this work, the authors report strong exciton-photon coupling modulated by the magnon-exciton coupling in a CrSBr
grating. Formation of polaritons with the grating bright and dark (BIC) modes have been experimentally extracted with large
coupling strength of 167 meV, consistent with previous reports in this material. The authors then demonstrated tuning of
these polariton modes with an applied external magnetic field in both static and pump-probe measurements. While the
attempt of fabricating nanophotonic devices that engineers the photonic band structures is applaudable, there are some
experimental observations that are potentially intriguing and worth further investigation, the data quality and analysis of the
current work need to be significantly improved. In particular, I think that the figures of the manuscripts are weakly connected
and there lacks a clear conclusion of how such devices can bring novel properties to the field and what are the implications.
First of all, in fig. 2 f&g, the experimental and simulation data are quite different in terms of the mode energy, linewidth, and
brightness, what is the reason of that? The fabrication process involved etching of the material, what is the quality of the
structure, such as roughness, homogeneity, sidewall angle, etc.? How are they deviates from the design and simulation
parameters? How was the exciton and other material properties affected by the etching? Are these the causes of the
deviation between the experiment and simulation?
Secondly, the phenomenon demonstrated in figure 3 is quite confusing. First, it is very hard to see the “Fano-like” feature the
authors mentioned that indicates the lightening up of the dark state, in either Fig. 3 d and e. It is quite confusing what are the
arrows pointing in the figure, as they are not aligned to any peaks or dips. Also, the experimental data is not in accordance with
the theory. As the authors mentioned, the dark mode at the Gamma point remained dark upon applying magnetic field,
as it is protected by the C2 symmetry, and thus the simulation in Fig. 3f corresponds to the reflectance data at 2.3 degree. In
this case, why the Gamma point data is shown in Fig. 3 d&e? Why is brightening of the dark state expected in these data?
Finally, what is the implication of this experiment?
Figure 4 demonstrates different angle-dependence of the acoustic and optical magnons, which is quite interesting. However,
the angle-resolved pump-probe reflectance data is noisy and needs improvements. The explanation about the difference
between the acoustic and optical magnons is quite preliminary and oversimplified. Is there any further theory or calculation
that can support the authors’ claim about the difference in momentum conservation in the optical and acoustic magnons?
Also, the authors mentioned that the optical magnons exhibit stronger coupling to excitons while the acoustic magnons has
much weaker coupling. However, in Fig. 4d, it seems that at near zero angles the signals originating from two types of
magnons have similar intensity, while at large angles the acoustic phonon dominates. Therefore the authors may want to
revise to a more precise description.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Overall, this manuscript presents a timely and original contribution to the emerging field of spin–photon interfaces based on
van der Waals magnetic semiconductors. By employing a CrSBr metasurface, the authors demonstrate that high-Q
resonances and exciton polariton bound states in the continuum (BICs) can be utilized to substantially enhance magnon–
photon interactions. The combination of steady-state optical spectroscopy and transient angle-resolved reflectance
measurements provides convincing evidence for magnon–exciton–photon hybridization and reveals mode- and momentum-
dependent dynamics that highlight direct momentum transfer from pump photons to magnons. These findings advance the
fundamental understanding of the interplay between spins, magnons, and photons in two-dimensional magnetic systems
and establish a promising platform for tunable, spin-dependent photonic and quantum devices.
That said, the current version requires further refinement before it can meet the publication standards of Nature
Communications. In particular, aspects of the experimental methodology, the theoretical interpretation, and the
contextualization within the broader literature should be clarified and strengthened.
1. Quoting “The CrSBr metasurface hosts an exciton polariton (EP) bound state in the continuum (BIC). Owing to the
magneto-electronic coupling effect of CrSBr and photonic singularity of the BIC mode, both the energy and the reflectivity of
the half-light, half-matter state can be efficiently tuned with an external magnetic field.” This statement in the Introduction
appears imprecise and somewhat misleading. Specifically, based on the one-dimensional CrSBr grating, the authors
investigate polaritons arising from the strong coupling between high-Q quasi-BICs and magnon–excitons in momentum
space, rather than a generic BIC-hosted polariton. To improve clarity, it would be important to provide a concise but accurate
introduction to the nonlocal BICs physics, with emphasis on how quasi-BIC resonances enhance light–matter interactions. In
particular, since exciton polaritons represent a local response while grating resonances are inherently nonlocal, the authors
should expand the Introduction to highlight the content of from local to nonlocal high-Q metasurfaces, supported by relevant
literature, so as to place this work more convincingly in the broader context of recent advances in photonic and polaritonic
metasurfaces.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Coherent control of light with electron spins represents a fundamental goal across multiple research fields, such as opto-spintronics, chiroptics, quantum information. In a magnetic-ordered material, coherent magnon gives rise to temporally and spatially modulated spin structure that may stimulate intriguing spin-photon interactions as well as opto-spintronic applications. However, the development of such magnon-photon interface is hampered due to the lack of magnetic photonic structure that embraces strong light-matter interaction. Here, we present such magnon-photon interface in a CrSBr metasurface by showing the formation of a magnetic exciton polariton bound states in the continuum, whose energy and the radiative properties can be tuned with an external magnetic field. We further show that the exciton polaritons are modulated by the coherent magnon excitation, exhibiting a nontrivial magnon mode- and k-dependent behavior which suggests the formation of hybrid magnon-exciton polariton states. Our results shed light on the interplay of spin, magnon and photon in the magnetic metasurface and provide a new platform for exploring spin functional photonic and quantum devices.

---

## Introduction

The electron spin carries non-volatile quantum information, which has been widely explored for information storage and processing1–5. Interfacing the spin states with photons allows communication and detection of spin quantum information over long distance6–9. Such spin-photon interface is therefore critical to connecting spatially separated quantum nodes and has been recognized as a vital part of the vision for scalable spin quantum information.

Significant progress has been made for non-magnetic spin-photon interface. This includes development of high-fidelity spin-photon entangled states, photons switches, routers and efficient chiral emitters controlled by electron spin in III-V semiconductor quantum dots7,9,10, transition metal dichalcogenide11–13 as well as scalable on-chip integration of optically active defect spins in diamond and SiC8,14,15. The non-magnetic semiconductor nanostructures and color centers are benefited from the optically active materials and long spin coherence time16,17. Whereas, magnetic materials, although being the backbone of contemporary spintronic research and memory industry, are less explored due to optically inactive band-edge transitions18,19, degraded optical properties20,21, as well as limited spin relaxation and coherence time22,23.

Recently, the discovery of magnetic semiconductors, e.g., CrSBr, with strong light-matter interaction and intriguing magneto-electronic coupling effect has revived the hope for developing a spin-photon interface that allows harvesting the versatility of spin manipulation and magnetic phase engineering in a magnetic material24–30. Additionally, magnon arises as a unique wave-like spin excitation in magnetically ordered materials31. In CrSBr, magnon is found strongly coupled to the excitonic states, reshaping its optical properties in the ultrafast timescale32,33. Despite the development, two major obstacles persist. First of all, studies of magnon-exciton interactions in 2D magnetic semiconductors have only been conducted in structureless samples which mostly involving interaction with free-space photons. Carefully designed photonic structures, e.g., photonic cavity or metasurfaces with high quality factor or strong magneto-optical response, will likely not only enhance the spin-photon interaction but also provide extra tunability34–36. In particular, photonic structures hosting bound states in the continuum (BICs) have attracted great attention due to their potential to achieve infinite-high cavity Q factors and sensitive to external perturbations, giving rise to intriguing light-matter interaction that facilitate the low threshold lasing, ultrafast optical switches, etc37–39. Coupling of the non-local BICs mode with the local excitation in the magnetic materials, e.g., excitons, may also give access to significant tunability through interplay of the local and non-local transition of the system40,41. Secondly, the fundamental physics underlying the coupling between collective spin waves and photons is not well understood. Although the propagation of magnons in CrSBr has been confirmed42,43, its interaction with the excitonic states is probed in a momentum-integrated manner. A momentum-resolved perspectives are therefore highly appreciated to shed light on the exotic nature of the magnon-photon coupling.

In this work, we demonstrate a magnon-photon interface based on a 1D metasurface of the magnetic semiconductor CrSBr. The CrSBr metasurface hosts BICs that are strongly coupled with excitons forming exciton polaritons (EPs). Owing to the magneto-electronic coupling effect of CrSBr and photonic singularity of the BICs mode, both the energy and the reflectivity of the half-light, half-matter state can be efficiently tuned with an external magnetic field. Furthermore, by performing the transient angle-resolved reflectance spectroscopy on the CrSBr metasurface, we find that the coherent magnon introduces a non-trivial k-dependent oscillation of EP energies that behaves differently for acoustic and optical magnons. These results highlight the wave nature of the magnon-photon coupling in the CrSBr metasurface, which establishes an innovative approach for controlling the photonic or polaritonic devices with electron spins.

---

## Results

Magnon-photon interface combining magneto-optical effect and photonic BICs

Figure 1a illustrates the proposed magnon-photon interface made from a CrSBr grating, in which the reflected light of frequency ωph and momentum k is coupled to the transverse electric (TE) mode of the grating and is modulated by a launched coherent magnon. The bulk CrSBr is an A-type antiferromagnetic semiconductor with Néel temperature TN = 132 K. The orientation of the antiferromagnetically coupled macrospins S1 and S2 in the adjacent layers has strong impact on the excitonic structure as well as optical response of the material. By applying an external magnetic field of B = 3 T along the c-axis, S1 and S2 switch from anti-parallel (AP) to parallel (P) spin configuration as shown in Fig. 1b. As a result, the b-axis dielectric function εb = ε1 + iε2 of CrSBr is modified drastically as shown in Fig. 1c, d. Here, εb is extracted from the reflectance spectra with details given in Supplementary Note 1 and Fig. S1. The multi-resonance reflectance features in Fig. S1 is due to the multi-order Fabry-Perot resonances arise from the planar cavity formed between the top and bottom surface of the CrSBr flake and is therefore not reflected by the fitted εb in Fig. 1c, d. The giant magneto-optical response is caused by spin mediated interlayer coupling, leading to a prominent redshift of the 1s exciton state from X(0) = 1.3643 eV to X(B) = 1.3485 eV as marked in Fig. 1d. Such magneto-electronic effect stems from the exchange interaction and is expected to have a stronger impact than typical magneto-optical effects, e.g., Faraday, Kerr rotation, etc., which are received from the spin orbital interaction44. In Fig. 1e, we show the calculated TE mode dispersion of the proposed CrSBr grating. Owing to the strong light-matter interaction, the shown eigenmodes are essentially EPs hybridized between the 1s exciton and guided resonances (GRs). The Γ point of the TE1 mode as marked in Fig. 1e is a BICs with topological charge C = +1, evidenced by divergent Q factor and the far-field polarization map as shown in Fig. 1f. The corresponding mode distribution can be found in Supplementary Fig. S2. The BICs mode is often considered as photonic singularity which is inherited with strong tunability. However, to our knowledge, its role in a magnetic metasurface as the one shown here has not yet been explored.

Strong coupling of exciton and BICs mode in a CrSBr 1D grating

The optical and atomic force microscopy (AFM) image of the exfoliated CrSBr flake is shown in Fig. 2a, b. The polarization-resolved photoluminescence (PL) spectra in Fig. 2c reveal emissions from a series of self-hybridized EPs that are linearly polarized along the b-axis. The coupling strength is estimated to be ~ 167 meV by fitting the emission peak position with a coupled oscillator model (COM) as shown in Fig. 2d (see Supplementary Note 2 and Fig. S3).

Next, the CrSBr metasurface is fabricated by patterning the CrSBr flakes with e-beam lithography followed by dry etching. The grating grooves are aligned along the b-axis of the crystal to maximize the coupling strength. In Fig. 2e, the scanning electron microscope (SEM) image shows that the bottom part of the CrSBr flake is still connected, allowing the continuous propagation of spin wave throughout the whole structure. Figure 2f shows the angle-resolved reflectance (ARR) spectrum taken from the CrSBr metasurface at 10 K, which is nicely matched to the simulated ARR spectrum in Fig. 2g. In Supplementary Fig. S4, we show the ARR spectrum from a CrSBr metasurface with the same structure parameters while the grating grooves are along a-axis. In this case, the photonic modes are decoupled from the exciton, giving rise to markedly different dispersion as in Fig. S4. Furthermore, we have carried out analysis based on COM and the simulation results are shown in Fig. S5. The COM suggests that a coupling strength of ~ 186 meV is needed to reproduce the observed polariton dispersion and the strong coupling is also reached in the CrSBr grating sample. We note that the slightly increase of the fitting values for the coupling strength as well as exciton oscillator strength (see table S1) for the CrSBr grating as compared to the bulk sample is likely artificially caused by the Lorentzian dielectric model25,26 which neglects the energy dependence of the background dielectric constant εb0. A more accurate determination of the coupling strength requires a more realistic modeling of the dielectric function over large spectral range. Nevertheless, the obtained comparable exciton oscillator strength for the etched and unetched sample suggest that the optical quality of the CrSBr grating is not compromised by etching. The EPs at around 1.27 eV in Fig. 2f features a bright and dark state (BS and DS) at Γ point (θ = 0) separated by a gap of ~ 8 meV. The same spectral feature is observed in the angle-resolved PL (ARPL) spectrum in Fig. 3a. The EPs emission intensity diminishes at the vicinity of the DS, accompanied by the increase of the Q factor as shown in Fig. 3b. The DS and BS are identified as the TE1 and TE2 EP. The two modes are slightly redshifted compared from the eigenmode calculation in Fig. 1e due to the presence of the SiO/Si substrate. The absence of the PL and reflectance contrast of the DS is due to the symmetry-forbidden emission of the BICs at θ = 0°. In the following content, we will refer to the exciton polariton formed by the strong coupling between the BICs mode and CrSBr excitons as EP BICs for short.

Tuning the exciton polariton BICs with magnetic field

The formation of EP BICs facilitates the control of its optical response by manipulating the spin configuration. Applying an out-of-plane magnetic field tilts the macrospins S1 and S2 as illustrated in Fig. 3c. The change of spin configuration modulates the energy of the EPs. As shown in Fig. 3d, the BS redshifts with magnetic field and reaches saturation at B = 2.1 T. The total energy change of the BS ΔEBS = 13.1 meV is huge considering the field induced total energy shift of 1s exciton is about 4Eex = 15.8 meV. The large energy shift is consistent with the substantial exciton fraction of the EP which is estimated |X|2 = (|X|2 + |C|2) = 0.39 using the coupled oscillator model. Here, X and C are the exciton and photon part of the Hopfield coefficients for the lower polariton branch45.

Interestingly, The EP BICs which is completely dark in the ARR measurement in the absence of magnetic field, start to red shifts and develops a reflectance feature with applying magnetic field. The brightening of EP BICs is further illustrated in Fig. 3e, where two resonant features are identified at B = 3 T and fitted with Fano lineshape. The dashed and solid arrows mark the fitted resonant energies of the bright and dark state. Table S2 in the supplementary information summarizes the fitting parameters for the two resonances. As guided by the fitting curves, the dark state locates at about 8 meV above the bright state and exhibits a highly asymmetric lineshape. As a comparison, only the resonant feature of the BS is observed and fitted for spectrum measured at B = 0 T in Fig. 3e.

An out-of-plane magnetic field contributes to a sizable off-diagonal dielectric tensor element εab = ε0ab + iε0ab (see Supplementary Note 3 and Fig. S6)46. εab introduces coupling between GRs and broad FP resonances, that can potentially affects the reflectance spectrum in field. Ideally the Γ-point BICs is strictly radiatively forbidden. The robustness of the BICs is protected by the C2 symmetry which holds even in the presence of magnetic field. This is shown with simulated reflectance spectrum in Fig. 3f in which the reflectance features of BICs is absent at different ε0ab for a perfect grating with infinite periods. However, the translation symmetry is broken due to limited sample size or white light spot size. As a result, the reflectance at θ = 0° mixes in the contributions from near-Γ quasi-BICs at finite k. Considering system dimension of ~ 20 μm limited by beam size, it leads to a k-space blurriness of Δθ ~ 1.4° as estimated with the uncertainty relation Δk · Δx ≥ 1/2. Such near-Γ contribution is simulated in Fig. 3g, h for θ = 0.3° and 0.6°. It is evident that the reflectance features of the quasi-BICs state (DS) gradually build up with the increase of ε0ab within the uncertainty limit of Δθ, which is consistent with the experimental observation of the brightened BICs in Fig. 3d and e. In Fig. S7, we further show from simulation that the field-induced reflectance features from the quasi-BICs depends on both real and imaginary part of εab and generally leads to asymmetric Fano lineshape as observed in the experiment. The observed intriguing magneto-optical effect emerges exclusively at the magnetic EP-BICs, which is due to the combined effect of the magnetic field induced εab and the fact that the quasi-BICs is sensitive to such external perturbation. In Supplementary Fig. S8, as a comparison, we show that the reflectance amplitude is barely changed for other EPs that are far apart from the BICs point.

k-dependent magnon-exciton polariton interaction

Next, we turn to the EPs that are closer to the exciton resonance which maximize the magnon-photon interaction. A transient ARR (tr-ARR) spectroscopy is employed to study the interaction between the EPs and coherent magnons in the CrSBr metasurface. The tr-ARR monitors the time evolution of the pump induced ARR change ΔR/R(θ, Eprobe) which are function of both the probe light energy Eprobe and θ. Our measurement configuration is shown in Fig. 4a. A constant magnetic field of 0.48 T is applied to cant the interlayer spins which facilitate exciton-magnon coupling25. Figure 4b shows a typical tr-ARR spectrum measured at 14 K and t = 47 ps. Here, the ΔR/R is mainly caused by pump induced redshift of the EPs, which is opposite to the typical blueshift observed for EPs nonlinearity in non-magnetic materials47,48. The effect is pronounced for EPs derived from the FP mode at around 1.35 eV and multiple GRs in between 1.3-1.34 eV. We attribute the ΔR/R signal to the excitation of incoherent magnon, which contributes to the decreases of EP energies and decays slowly with time as shown in Supplementary Fig. S9. Apart from the incoherent component, the coherent magnon excitation is also observed as the temporal oscillation of the ΔR/R. In the upper panel of Fig. 4c, the coherent oscillation of the tr-ARR (CoTR) is made pronounced by taking the time derivative of ΔR/R and is plotted as function of Eprobe and t for θ = 0°. The oscillations take opposite phase for Eprobe above and below the EP resonances. It suggests that the EP energies are periodically modulated through interaction with coherent magnon, which is consistent with previous report in pristine CrSBr flakes32. In the lower panel of Fig. 4c, CoTR at probe energy (Eprobe = 1.3536 eV) slightly above the 1.35-eV EP is plotted against time, exhibiting clear oscillations with a beating amplitude.

To gain in-depth understanding of the coherent magnon-EP dynamics, we performed fast Fourier transformation (FFT) of the CoTR signal for each Eprobe and the results for different θ are shown in Fig. 4e. In the FFT spectra, two dominant oscillation frequencies at 30 GHz and 22 GHz are identified and attributed to the acoustic and optical magnon modes (marked as Ac. and Op.). The corresponding mode character featured by the in-phase and out-of-phase precession of the macrospin S1 and S2 of the neighboring antiferromagnetically coupled layers is illustrated in Fig. 4d. In Fig. 4f, the FFT magnitude at the two magnon mode frequencies is plotted against θ. The FFT magnitude at the frequency of optical magnon decreases at higher |θ|, whereas the acoustic magnon contribution remains at a comparable level for all θ in our measurements. The k-dependent coupling between EP and optical magnon modes cannot be otherwise explained by any k-space dependence of the EP, which is shown to be similar for both magnon modes. It has been suggested that the transient strain field generated by the pump light plays important roles for launching magnon in CrSBr and the k-space distribution of the coherent magnon should be limited by the Fourier transformation of the real-space transient strain field42. In our measurement, the pump laser was defocused to a large laser spot size of ~ 10 μm. It therefore generates a broad real-space heat/strain profile. The dashed line in Fig. 4f estimate the contribution of heat/strain by showing the Fourier transformation of the real-space laser spot profile, which is too narrow to account for the observation of the broad k-space profile for the optical magnon. It suggests that the EP oscillations ΔE(t) ∝ Δm(t) ∝ Δm(t) where ΔE(t) is the relative angle between S1(t) and S2(t) for the exciton energy difference between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phase. The magnon-photon interactions observed here are beyond the conventional heat/strain-mediated mechanism which is often responsible for magnon-photon interaction in magnetic materials or devices. Furthermore, the optical magnon has a similar profile as the angular distribution of the pump density (Fig. 4f). It is worth to know that such angular distribution of the pump density deviates from the Fourier transformed real-space profile of the pump beam due to the defocused pump laser beam setting. This is a strong indication for a k-conserved coupling between EP and the optical magnons such that the momentum is transferred to the magnon mode upon optical excitation. However, such momentum conservation law does not hold for acoustic magnons. We note that the similar k-conserved behavior of the optical magnon is also observed for measurement in pristine CrSBr as shown in Fig. 4g, h. However, a noteworthy difference in the unpatterned CrSBr is that the acoustic mode is absent in the FFT spectra at all angles.

To shed light on the different k-space behavior of the optical and acoustic magnons, we solved the Landau-Lifshitz equation describing the time evolution of sublattice magnetization mi=1,2(t) of bulk CrSBr as illustrated in Fig. 5a,

dmi(t)/dt = -γμ0 mi(t) × Hi,eff (1)

Here, γ and μ0 are gyromagnetic ratio and vacuum permeability. Hi,eff is the effective magnetic field of mi=1,2(t) and includes contributions from Zeeman interaction, interlayer exchange coupling and the magnetic anisotropy (detailed derivation is given in Supplementary Note 4). Assuming the reported interaction parameters, Fig. 5b shows the calculated mode frequencies for acoustic and optical magnons as function of the c-axis magnetic field32. It is established that the modulation of the CrSBr exciton and exciton polariton energies ΔE is proportional to the time-varying angle between S1(t) and S2(t). Figure 5c, d calculate the temporal modulation of ΔE at zero and finite magnetic field assuming either acoustic or optical magnon is excited. At Hext = 0, neither acoustic nor optical magnon is coupled to the exciton or EPs, as evidenced by the absence of ΔE at the magnon frequency ω in Fig. 5c. However, weak higher order frequency component at 2ω is identified for both magnons. A finite magnetic field, e.g., μ0Hext = 0.48 T, initiates the coupling between the exciton and the optical mode as shown by the emerging oscillation of ΔE at ω in Fig. 5d. Whereas, the acoustic mode remains decoupled at frequency ω. Such distinct selection rules for acoustic and optical magnons in bulk CrSBr nicely explain the absence of the acoustic magnon in the FFT spectra for the unetched CrSBr sample (Fig. 4g, h). The observation of disallowed acoustic magnon in the FFT spectra for CrSBr grating (Fig. 4e, f) then must arise from the etched edges and sidewalls which have low symmetry. At such localized site, the acoustic magnon-exciton polariton interaction therefore does not conserve k and naturally leads to an insensitive dependence on angle. On the other hand, the selection-rules-allowed optical mode requires match of momentum owing to the preserved translation symmetry and therefore leads to an angle-sensitive behavior for both the pristine CrSBr flake and the CrSBr grating. The mode- and k-dependent magnon-EP interaction may indicate the formation of strongly coupled EP-magnon hybrid such that a k-selected excitation of the EPs directly leads to the k-dependent pumping of the coherent magnons which in turn modulates the EPs energies. Such mechanism is therefore sensitive to the character of the magnons in the way that favors the direct optical magnon-EP coupling through the induced angle change between adjacent interlayer macrospins.

We note that controlling light with electron spins has strong implications in spin quantum information and spintronics, which is generally difficult for conventional meta-surfaces or polaritonic devices based on non-magnetic materials. Towards such goal, we have demonstrated both static and ultrafast control of exciton polariton with electron spin or collective modes of spins in a magnetic photonic structure of CrSBr, by harnessing the synergistic interplay between strong light-matter interactions and magneto-electronic effects. Furthermore, the observation of 2D magnon mode- and k-dependent EP interaction provides a compelling evidence of direct momentum transfer from pump photons to the optical magnons, suggesting the formation of strongly coupled magnon-EP hybrid state. These findings provide valuable information for the spin- and magnon-photon interactions in the 2D limit and open a new gateway for exploring spin functional photonic and quantum devices with 2D magnetic semiconductors.

---

## Methods

Fabrication of CrSBr metasurface
The commercially available CrSBr crystal (from Nanjing MKNANO) was mechanically exfoliated onto a silicon substrate with a 300-nm oxide layer in the glove box, and the thickness was determined using AFM. Electron beam lithography and ICP-RIE were used to partially etch CrSBr, forming a one-dimensional grating. The etched area of the CrSBr flake is 30 μm × 30 μm. The grating structural parameters and roughness of the measured grating sample is characterized by SEM and AFM in Fig. S10.

Angle-resolved reflectance and PL spectroscopy
The optical measurements are conducted with samples loaded into a low-vibration closed-cycle cryostat. For the PL measurement, a 532-nm continue-wave laser was used for excitation. A halogen lamp was used for the reflectance measurement. The PL emission and the reflected light were collected with a long-working-distance objective lens with a numerical aperture of 0.42. The angle-resolved reflectance/PL spectroscopy consists of reflectance/PL spectra for different incidence angle θ, which are performed by projecting the back focal plane of the objective lens to a spectrometer (FHR640) equipped with a Si charge coupled device (CCD) camera.

Transient angle-resolved reflectance spectroscopy
The tr-ARR measurements are performed with a home-built set-up, which is schematically shown in supplementary Fig. S11. A 1-kHz 800-nm pulsed laser is used as pump light. The pulse width is about 150 fs. The probe light is the white light generated by pumping a sapphire plate with the fs laser. The delay time t between the pump light and the white probe light is precisely controlled to yield the time evolution of ΔR/R. The pump energy density is kept low at 5.1 pJ/μm2 to avoid compromising the coherence of the exciton-magnon coupling due to high carrier/exciton density. The pump light intensity is modulated at the frequency of 20 Hz and the k-space image of the pump induced reflectance change is dispersed and recorded with an EMCCD camera (from Raptor Photonics) that is synchronized to the modulation speed. The pump and probe light spot size is about 10 μm.

Numerical simulations
The finite element method (FEM) is employed to simulate the eigenvalues and reflectance spectra of CrSBr photonic structures using a commercially available software (COMSOL Multiphysics). Periodic boundary conditions are applied in the x- and y-directions, while perfectly matched layers (PMLs) are implemented in the z-direction to minimize reflections. The optical anisotropy of the material is modeled using a dielectric tensor,

ε = [εa 0 0; 0 εb 0; 0 0 εc]

where εa = 12, εc = 3.7. To simulate the eigen-energy of polariton bands, the εb is approximated with the Lorentzian mode:

εb(ω) = εb0 + f/(ω2 - iωΓ - E2X/ℏ2) + f*/(ω2 - iωΓ* - E2X*/ℏ2)

with εb0 = 11.1. The contribution of exciton resonance is taken into account with following parameters, EX = 1.364 eV, EX* = 1.379 eV, ℏΓ = 0.7 meV, ℏΓ* = 7.5 meV, ℏf = 1.304 eV, ℏf* = 0.707 eV. The wave equation,

∇ × (∇ × E(ω)) = k20ε(ω)E(ω)

is then solved numerically by matching the frequency of the eigen mode E(ω) with the dielectric function dispersion ε(ω).

To simulate the magneto-optical effect, an off-diagonal gyromagnetic term is introduced into the dielectric tensor as46,

ε = [εa εab 0; -εab εb 0; 0 0 εc]
